I have been farming these 16.1 mu for twenty years now. I know every corner of my plots. My household has seven mouths, and some of my children work off-farm in the city, so I cannot rely on too much family labor during the busy seasons. I have a well, which means I can irrigate when the rains fail, but pumping water costs diesel and money, so I do not water more than I must.

It is early spring now. My winter wheat is already in the ground from last October. I will manage it the way I always have: I will topdress with urea at green-up and again at jointing, and I will run the rotary tiller between rows to break the crust after the winter. I will irrigate three times—once now to wake the crop up, once at heading, and once during grain filling. I will spray insecticide twice and herbicide once, and if I see rust I will add a fungicide. I expect about 1,000 jin per mu from the wheat, which is decent and reliable.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize. I always buy hybrid seed from the county shop—those seeds grow fast and strong in the short summer window. I will not till much; I will plant directly into the wheat stubble to save time and labor before the rains come. I will put down compound fertilizer at planting and side-dress with urea when the plants are knee-high. Two irrigations will be enough if the summer rains are normal, and I will spray for pests three times. I expect around 1,150 jin per mu from the maize.

For cotton, I keep 4.1 mu on the sandier plot. I will rotary-till in April and plant my improved cotton seed. Cotton needs patience and many sprays—about thirteen applications through the season for bollworm, aphids, and weeds—but the price is usually better than grain, and my wife can help pick it in autumn. I will irrigate twice and fertilize with compound fertilizer at planting and once more at flowering. I hope for 600 jin of seed cotton per mu.

At my age, I do not experiment. I do what the land and my well allow. The wheat and maize keep us fed and bring steady cash, while the cotton gives us a bit extra for my grandchildren's school fees.
